newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks welcome U.S. election, more gains seen.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks welcome U.S. election, more gains seen.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks stormed into record territory on Wednesday and are poised for more gains, analysts said, with U.S. election results pointing to a friendly interest-rate outlook.
The Hang Seng index surged 272.77 points or 2.18 percent to a record close of 12,775.47 after hitting an intra-day record high at 12,779.11 on the election results.
"The re-election of Bill Clinton and the Republicans controlling Congress -- that is the best result that the market was expecting," said Ken Chan, senior economist at Nikko Research Centre.

"The Republicans getting control of Congress will mean that there will be little change in (economic) policy, so basically the market is expecting no interest-rate hike this year," Chan said. "Although we might see some profit-taking, the general trend is going up."
David Semple, equity strategist at Peregrine Research Institute, said Democratic control of Congress could have prompted a decline in U.S. stock prices.
"You have the same man in the White House and the same Congressmen and that is very good news for bonds and I think that obviously creates a better interest-rate environment in the region," he said.
"It has removed one of the uncertainties. In Hong Kong it means that interest rates are stable," Semple added.
Chan said the Hong Kong economy could also benefit from improving ties between China and the Clinton administration.

"The relationship with China would reduce the possibility of a trade dispute with China. It would benefit China in terms of the bid for WTO (World Trade Organisation) membership and that would help China's trade so Hong Kong will benefit," he said.
The Hang Seng index is up 26.8 percent this year as of Wednesday's close. Analysts said the 13,000-point mark appeared to be the next target for the blue-chip barometer.
"It looks like the market has the momentum to go higher. I don't think we should have any difficulty going to 13,000 in the near term," said Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International.
However, Grant Forster, vice president at BT Fund Managers, said the favourable outcome seemed to have been discounted.

"This is the favourable outcome for bonds. But that has now been built into the market," he said. "People will again start turning to the next set of jobs figures and the next Federal Reserve policy meeting," he said.
But Forster said as long as the interest-rate environment remains friendly the Hong Kong market should remain buoyant.
Semple said the Hang Seng index could reach 13,500 points in February or March before leveling off.
